summary: El Grande is a tense area-majority game where lords place knights across Spanish regions to seize control at three scoring checkpoints. Much of the tension comes from bidding on power cards for turn order and secretly committing knights to the castillo before big reveals.
praised: tense simultaneous bidding for turn order
criticised: can feel mean and swingy when majorities flip late
King placement by the last player can feel arbitrary

interaction.kind: Area-majority battles over shared regions plus bidding for turn order/action strength
interaction.detail: Every round players bid (via power cards) for turn order and caballero supply, then place knights directly into the same nine regions to contest majority, often specifically to bump a rival out of first or second place. The board state is almost entirely shared — your own 'engine' barely exists outside the regions everyone is fighting over.
interaction.said: Frequently called one of the most confrontational euros ever made — "a fight over the same nine regions," "you're always reading what everyone else is about to do," "the king screws you as much as your opponents do"

scoring.how_you_win: Across scorings after rounds 3, 6 and 9, hold the most (or 2nd/3rd most) caballeros in each region to bank points; the highest cumulative total after round 9 wins.

theme.said: frequently cited as the archetypal 'pasted-on theme' euro, 'medieval Spain wallpaper on a cube-majority game,' 'could be about painting fences and nothing would change'
theme.why: caballeros are undifferentiated cubes contested for regional majority scoring, and nothing about knights, courts, or Spanish nobility explains why moving a stat-based number of cubes from a court into a region determines control, since any area-majority theme would produce the identical ruleset

style.why: An auction-driven action-point economy with symmetric caballero placement and scoring at fixed intervals, softened only by blocking and modest hidden-bid uncertainty rather than true conflict or luck
